label: SLA vs MOU vs MOA vs MSA vs SOW vs NDA vs BPA

mentor.diagnosis: You matched on a vague sense of 'contract' rather than on what each document actually fixes.
contrast: Measurable service levels: uptime, response time, penalties
A shared understanding of intent between parties
Agreed roles and responsibilities, more formal than an MOU
The umbrella terms governing an ongoing relationship
The specific deliverables and timeline for one piece of work
How two businesses will operate a joint venture, including profit sharing
mentor.rule: MSA is the umbrella, SOW is the individual job under it. SLA is the measurable promise. MOU is intent without teeth.
mentor.tell: Any number with a unit, such as 99.9% or four hours, means SLA. 'Deliverables and milestones for this project' means SOW.
mentor.trap: MOU and MOA differ by one letter and are both about mutual understanding. MOU is intent, MOA adds defined responsibilities and is normally binding.

label: Right-to-audit clause vs independent assessment vs questionnaire vs supply chain analysis

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a vendor assurance method that does not give the level of confidence the scenario asked for.
contrast: The vendor's own answers about its controls
Better, still the vendor auditing itself
A third party's report, such as SOC 2
Strong, and on the vendor's schedule and scope
A contractual right for YOU to audit them
Strongest, on your schedule and your scope
Visibility into the vendor's own suppliers
mentor.rule: A right-to-audit clause must be negotiated into the contract before signing. Afterwards you get whatever the vendor chooses to share.
mentor.tell: 'We must be able to inspect their controls ourselves, at a time of our choosing' is a right-to-audit clause.
mentor.trap: A SOC 2 report is genuinely independent and is the usual answer, but its scope and timing are chosen by the vendor. When the stem stresses your control over the review, it is the right-to-audit clause.

label: Due diligence before, monitoring during, and who is independent enough to assess

mentor.diagnosis: You treated third-party risk as a thing you do once, at signing. The objectives split it across the relationship, and separately care about whether whoever assessed the vendor had a reason to be kind.
contrast: Should we engage this supplier at all
What the vendor says about itself
What the vendor's own assurance function found, graded by the vendor
What a third party with no stake found
Whether you may go and look yourself
Whether the vendor's controls survive an attacker
Has anything changed since we assessed them
mentor.rule: Due diligence is a decision about entering a relationship. Monitoring is how you notice it has changed. A vendor assessed once at signing is a vendor you know nothing current about.
mentor.tell: A supplier breached years into a relationship points to monitoring. A supplier being selected points to due diligence.
mentor.trap: A conflict of interest invalidates the assessment regardless of its findings. An assessor paid by the vendor, or one who also sells them remediation, is not independent, and the exam expects you to notice that before reading the conclusion.
